strengths: The manuscript studies an important problem: post-hoc calibration of full regression distributions under the stronger auto-calibration criterion rather than only marginal PIT uniformity.

The oracle construction Q̃=P(Y|Q) is conceptually clean, and the proper-score decomposition clearly connects calibration error, grouping loss/lack of sharpness, and irreducible uncertainty. The paper appropriately acknowledges its connection to prior grouping-loss results.
Estimating P(Y|Q) with conditional kernel mean embeddings is flexible across predictive model classes, and experiments cover four base-model families and eleven datasets over 20 splits.

The empirical evaluation considers both calibration and predictive quality through SKCE, PIT testing, CRPS, and a conformal-prediction comparison. The paper also reports computational scaling and openly discusses cubic calibration-set complexity, lack of feature-conditional calibration, and loss of continuous-density structure.

The manuscript is generally well organized and includes proofs, algorithms, detailed per-dataset results, and an honest limitations section. weaknesses: The central guarantee does not apply to the implemented algorithm. Proposition 5.2 establishes auto-calibration and sharpness preservation only for the inaccessible population object P(Y|Q). The CKME estimate is subsequently converted into a distribution by projecting its coefficients onto the Euclidean simplex, whereas the actual pre-image objective uses the target-kernel Gram matrix. No theorem bounds the error introduced by this approximation or establishes calibration, consistency, or sharpness preservation for the final projected empirical distribution. Consequently, statements that the algorithm “enforces” auto-calibration or preserves sharpness are unsupported.

The cited CKME consistency result is insufficient to close this gap: its assumptions and required regularization schedule are not stated, cross-validated regularization is not connected to those assumptions, and consistency of an RKHS embedding does not automatically imply consistency after the manuscript's altered pre-image projection in the calibration quantities being claimed.

The main empirical evidence treats failure to reject the SKCE null as evidence that calibration was achieved. Acceptance rates, especially with test sets as small as 31–160 examples, can largely reflect low power. The paper gives neither SKCE effect sizes nor confidence intervals, power simulations, or comparisons under known calibrated and controlled-miscalibrated alternatives. Figure 1 therefore does not justify the strong conclusion that calibration error was corrected.

Evaluation is unusually aligned with the proposed method: SKCE uses the proposed Energy Distance Kernel over distributions, while CKME is built from the same distribution geometry. Results with independent characteristic kernels, bandwidth sensitivity analyses, or other strong calibration diagnostics are needed to show that the improvement is not specific to this metric/kernel choice.

The GPBETA comparison is compromised by replacing every non-Gaussian base prediction with a Gaussian fitted to its first two moments because of limitations of the chosen implementation. This discards precisely the multimodal or empirical-distribution information that CKME retains, so it cannot support a broad state-of-the-art superiority claim. No comparable modern nonparametric/local calibration baseline is included.

Predictive-quality results are mixed. CKME substantially worsens CRPS in several cases—for example, GDN/MDN/BNN on Yacht and Housing—and the model trained on the combined training and calibration data is frequently better. There are no paired significance tests or uncertainty estimates for method differences beyond across-split standard deviations. Thus the claims of consistent superiority and preserved usefulness are overstated.

The claimed originality is limited: the core algorithm is conditional distribution regression from Q to Y using a standard CKME estimator; the Gaussian-of-energy-distance construction follows established Gaussian-type distribution kernels and known energy-distance/MMD computations; and the decomposition quantitatively matches prior grouping-loss work. The paper needs a sharper account of what is technically new and a more complete proof for that new component.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript itself. Base-model architectures, optimization settings, distribution sample sizes, exact hyperparameter grids, SKCE resampling/test details, and compute requirements for the full benchmark are not adequately specified. A code link is asserted but absent in the anonymized manuscript, so the reported results cannot presently be reconstructed from the paper alone.

The presentation is mostly clear, but several plots are too dense to read comfortably and some statements need correction or qualification, including the apparent typo I(I;X) and the claim that auto-calibration implies ordinary PIT uniformity despite the proposed output being discrete unless a randomized PIT is used.

There is no evident harmful-data or human-subject concern, but the impact statement is boilerplate despite repeated safety-critical motivation. The work should explicitly warn that auto-calibration is weaker than feature-conditional or subgroup calibration and that passing a low-powered test is not a deployment guarantee. The limitations section notes the former issue but does not reconcile it with the high-stakes framing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: PIT calibration is only marginal and can conceal prediction-dependent overconfidence and underconfidence. Targeting auto-calibration is well motivated, particularly for uncertainty-sensitive applications.

The oracle recalibration map Q -> P(Y|Q) and the proper-score decomposition provide a useful conceptual account of calibration versus information loss. The connection to grouping loss is clearly discussed and the main oracle-level propositions are supported by proofs.

Using conditional kernel mean embeddings produces a flexible recalibration framework that can accommodate non-Gaussian predictive distributions. The experiments cover four base-model families and eleven datasets over 20 repetitions.

The manuscript is generally readable, well structured, and candid about cubic scaling, empirical rather than density-valued outputs, and the fact that auto-calibration remains weaker than feature-conditional calibration.
weaknesses: Soundness: the main guarantee applies to the inaccessible oracle P(Y|Q), not to Algorithm 2. The implemented method first estimates a conditional mean embedding and then replaces the proper RKHS pre-image optimization in Eq. 39 with an additional Euclidean simplex projection in Eq. 40. No theorem or finite-sample bound shows that this approximation is consistent, preserves sharpness, or approaches auto-calibration. Thus statements that the algorithm “enforces” auto-calibration and preserves sharpness are unsupported.

Soundness: the empirical argument repeatedly treats failure to reject the SKCE null as evidence of calibration. Figure 1 reports acceptance frequencies, including test sets as small as 31, 51, and 77 observations, where power is plainly limited. A diffuse or nearly constant predictor can also be auto-calibrated while losing useful information. Neither high p-values nor frequent non-rejection establishes that CKME corrected calibration, yet Section 6.4 and the conclusion make precisely that inference.

Soundness: sharpness preservation is not evaluated. The paper acknowledges that it cannot estimate sharpness and substitutes CRPS, which conflates calibration and sharpness. Table 1 shows substantial CKME degradation in multiple settings—for example relative CRPS 1.276/1.326/1.614 on Yacht for GDN/MDN/BNN and 1.150/1.175/1.188 on Housing—so the claim that CKME usually marginally improves the score and preserves useful predictions is overstated.

Evaluation fairness is questionable. GPBETA can officially operate only on Gaussian outputs, so the authors Gaussianize all other base-model predictions before applying it. This discards multimodality and distributional structure and handicaps the comparator; results for these combinations do not support superiority over GPBETA. At minimum, conclusions should be restricted to naturally compatible Gaussian base models or use suitable nonparametric baselines.

The claim of consistent empirical superiority is contradicted by Table 1. CKME is often worse in CRPS than the unrecalibrated model, training on the combined train/calibration data, or PIT recalibration, especially for neural base models. No paired statistical tests or uncertainty for method differences are given, and the many dataset/model comparisons raise multiplicity concerns.

The PIT evaluation is under-specified for CKME's discrete empirical predictive distributions. Ordinary PIT values are not uniform for discontinuous CDFs without randomized PIT or another discrete calibration construction, but the manuscript does not state how ties and jumps are handled. The exact SKCE estimator, resampling/null-calibration procedure, and number of resamples are also omitted.

Originality is moderate rather than compelling. CKME distribution regression, Gaussian-type kernels over mean embeddings, the Brownian/energy-distance equivalence, and fast univariate energy-distance computation are established ingredients. The Energy Distance Kernel appears largely to be a direct instantiation of these results, and the claimed novelty is not sharply separated from prior work.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript. It says the experiment code is publicly available but provides a blank location, with similar missing links in several appendices. Architectures, training procedures, predictive-sample counts, optimization grids, randomization details, and complete calibration-test settings are insufficiently specified. The runtime comparison also uses GPU-accelerated CKME against an explicitly expensive PIT implementation and covers only two base-model families, limiting its interpretability.

Presentation: the exposition is clear at a high level, but several claims are stronger than the evidence. In particular, “comprehensive,” “consistently outperforms,” “validating the theoretical foundations,” and safety-critical applicability are not warranted by small tabular benchmarks and low-powered goodness-of-fit tests. There is also a factor-of-two imprecision when Eq. 4 is identified as the conventional energy distance.

Limitations and ethics: the limitations section usefully acknowledges computational and output-representation issues, but omits the central statistical limitations—lack of a finite-sample calibration guarantee, low test power, possible loss of sharpness, bounded calibration-set support, and distribution shift. Given the safety-critical framing, the generic impact statement should explicitly caution that benchmark non-rejection does not establish deployment reliability. No separate material ethical violation is evident, but the deployment rhetoric is insufficiently qualified.

strengths: Soundness: The population target, recalibrating Q to P(Y|Q), is well motivated, and Proposition 5.2 clearly establishes auto-calibration and preservation of sharpness for this oracle map. The proper-score decomposition provides a useful conceptual account of calibration, sharpness, and aleatoric uncertainty.

Empirical evidence is broad: 11 datasets, four substantially different probabilistic-regression model classes, 20 repetitions, two calibration tests, CRPS, and comparisons with PIT, GPBETA, conformal prediction, and unrecalibrated alternatives. CKME is particularly convincing on the larger test sets in the SKCE results, where low test power is less concerning.

The proposed CKME recalibration is a useful nonparametric alternative to moment-based parametric maps. The energy-distance distribution kernel is computationally valuable for empirical univariate predictions, and the runtime ablation supports its practical advantage.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The paper explains why PIT calibration is insufficient, separates calibration from predictive score, provides readable algorithms, and includes detailed per-dataset results in the appendix.

The limitations discussion is appropriately candid about cubic calibration-set scaling, the gap between auto-calibration and feature-conditional calibration, and loss of continuous-density structure. These admissions should not count against the paper.

weaknesses: The strongest theoretical guarantee applies to the inaccessible population map P(Y|Q), not directly to the implemented algorithm. CKME estimates only its embedding, after which the method replaces the RKHS pre-image optimization with Euclidean projection onto the simplex. The paper does not prove that this additional approximation is consistent or preserves auto-calibration or sharpness. Thus statements that the algorithm "enforces" auto-calibration are stronger than what is established.

The empirical calibration claim relies mainly on failure to reject SKCE or PIT null hypotheses. Null acceptance is not affirmative evidence of calibration, especially for test sets as small as 31–160 examples. Reporting SKCE effect estimates, confidence intervals, and power analyses would make the evidence substantially more persuasive.

Predictive-quality gains are mixed rather than consistent. Table 1 shows CKME materially worsening CRPS for several model-dataset pairs, particularly Yacht and Housing, while training the base model on the combined training and calibration data is often competitive or better. This limits the practical case when calibration data could instead improve the underlying model.

The GPBETA comparison is imperfect because non-Gaussian base predictions are first reduced to moment-matched Gaussians. That may discard information and weaken the closest parametric competitor; results should be separated for natively Gaussian models or supplemented with stronger distributional recalibration baselines.

Originality is meaningful but moderate: CKME regression, Gaussian kernels over distribution embeddings, energy-distance embeddings, and the grouping-loss decomposition are established ingredients. The contribution is primarily their synthesis into a recalibration pipeline and its evaluation; the paper should more precisely distinguish the genuinely new kernel result from known constructions.

Reproducibility is only adequate. Code availability is asserted, but the manuscript omits several operational details, including complete base-model architectures and training settings, preprocessing, seeds, the exact regularization search space, and some sampling choices. Runtime comparisons also use GPU acceleration for CKME and implementation-dependent sampling for PIT, reducing their generality.

The impact statement is cursory given the repeated safety-critical motivation. There are no apparent human-subject, privacy, or dual-use concerns in the reported benchmark study, but deployment risks from finite-sample or distribution-shift miscalibration deserve explicit discussion.
